title: Cranberry Sauce

drivers.name: Price increase (2.1%) with no promotion
drivers.evidence: Past promotions at deeper discounts show no sustained lift (noise-adjusted x1.0); price increase without promotion typically reduces demand, especially with supply risk.

drivers.name: Supplier delivery short warning
drivers.evidence: Supply risk likely leads to reduced consumer demand due to out-of-stocks; planner note indicates real concern.

adjustment.analysis: No events or promotions are scheduled. The price is up 2.1%, which historically has not driven lift (past promotions show noise-adjusted x1.0). The supplier warning of short delivery suggests supply risk, which may suppress demand. The baseline already reflects seasonal trends and recent volatility. No past Halloween effect is reliable (noise-adjusted x1.0). The classical model suggests no lift, and evidence supports no adjustment. A price increase without promotion or event, combined with supply risk, implies demand may dip slightly.

PRODUCT: Cranberry Sauce | category Grocery | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-25 (2 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 2.91 (+2.1% vs regular price 2.85)
  planner notes: Supplier warns of a short delivery

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 9.1 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 19.9 | 10%-90%: 1.9 - 17.3

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-81% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
